title: Language core: strings, immutability and memory (Java)
seriesTitle: Interview roadmap: Java and Spring Boot
seriesDescription: Java and Spring Boot interview topics in JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short Java/SQL code and multi-correct questions. Java only: nothing here mixes in Python.
description: String pool and == vs equals, StringBuilder, immutable classes, heap vs stack, generations, G1 and Metaspace, reference types, leak causes, reachability and shallow array clones.
source: JLS 3.10.5, 15.18.1 and 15.29; Oracle JVM GC Tuning Guide; JEP 122 (Metaspace) and JEP 248 (G1 default for server-class machines in JDK 9); java.lang.ref docs; Effective Java (Bloch) items 17, 50; Baeldung; Toptal interview list

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: A Java String can be shared between threads without any synchronization.
questions.reason: A String caches its hash code after the first call to hashCode().

whys.a: R is true, but caching is a performance detail that does not make sharing safe.
whys.b: Correct: both true; thread safety comes from immutability (final state), which also makes the cached hash safe, but caching does not cause it.
whys.c: R is true: String stores a hash field.
whys.d: A is true: immutable objects are inherently thread-safe.

questions.explanation: Immutability buys thread safety, safe use as map keys, string pooling and security (a validated path cannot change after the check).

questions.prompt: Given an int n, write Java that builds the string "0,1,2,...,n-1" (no trailing comma) in a variable s, using a StringBuilder instead of repeated + on a String.
questions.explanation: Using s += i in a loop creates a new String each iteration, which is O(n squared) in total. String.join or Collectors.joining are the stream alternatives; StringBuffer is the synchronized, slower older sibling.

questions.prompt: Complete the sentence about Java strings.
questions.text: Because String is {1}, literals can be shared from the string {2}, and its {3} can be cached after the first computation.
questions.explanation: The pool lives in the heap since Java 7. Immutability is a design choice enforced by a final class with private final fields, not by the final keyword on a variable.

questions.prompt: Declaring a variable final in Java (final List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();) makes the list it refers to immutable.

options.text: True
options.why: final only fixes the reference.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: you can still call names.add(...); final prevents reassigning the variable, not mutating the object.

questions.explanation: For real immutability use List.of / Collections.unmodifiableList (a view) or List.copyOf (a copy).

questions.prompt: Select all steps that are part of making a Java class truly immutable.

options.text: Declare the class final (or make constructors private) so subclasses cannot add mutability.
options.why: A subclass could otherwise override getters or add mutable state.

options.text: Make all fields private and final.
options.why: The core of immutability: fields set once in the constructor.

options.text: Provide no setters or other mutators.
options.why: No method may change observable state after construction.

options.text: Copy mutable inputs and outputs, such as a Date or List, defensively.
options.why: Otherwise callers keep a handle on the internal state.

options.text: Implement Serializable.
options.why: Unrelated to immutability and it adds extra concerns.

options.text: Mark every getter synchronized.
options.why: Unneeded: nothing changes after construction, so there are no races.

questions.explanation: Records automate most of this, but remember they are only shallowly immutable: a record with a List component is only immutable if you copy the list with List.copyOf.

questions.prompt: Match each JVM term with its description.

right.text: Eden plus survivor spaces; collected by frequent, short minor GCs
Holds objects that survived several collections; collected less often
Class metadata stored in native memory (replaced PermGen in Java 8)
Region-based collector with a pause-time target, default since JDK 9
Per-thread frames holding local variables and call state
Pool of interned string literals only

questions.explanation: Generational GC exploits the fact that most objects die young; stacks are per thread and freed on return.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: A Java application can leak memory even though it runs a garbage collector.
questions.reason: The garbage collector frees every object that is still reachable from a static collection.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Correct: A is true (unwanted but reachable objects are never collected); R is false, since reachable objects are never freed.

questions.explanation: GC reclaims unreachable objects only. A leak in Java means unintended reachability.

questions.prompt: Select all common causes of memory leaks in a long-running Java service.

options.text: A static Map used as a cache with no eviction or size bound.
options.why: It lives as long as the class, so entries are always reachable.

options.text: Listeners or callbacks registered but never deregistered.
options.why: The publisher keeps a strong reference (the lapsed listener problem).

options.text: ThreadLocal values never removed in a pooled thread.
options.why: Pool threads live forever, so their ThreadLocal map keeps the values.

options.text: Local variables inside a method that has already returned.
options.why: Their stack frame is gone, so they no longer keep objects alive.

options.text: Allocating many short-lived objects in the young generation.
options.why: This is what the young generation is designed for; it does not leak.

questions.explanation: Diagnose with a heap dump (jmap, VisualVM, Eclipse MAT): look for the dominator tree and the GC roots keeping the objects alive.

The variable a still references the first node, so it stays alive. After a.next = null nothing reaches b or c; their mutual cycle does not keep them reachable, so both are eligible: 2. Java uses reachability from GC roots, not reference counting.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: In Java, a local variable of reference type lives on the thread stack, while the object it points to lives on the heap.
questions.reason: Stack frames vanish when a method returns, whereas heap objects are reclaimed only by the garbage collector.

whys.a: Correct: the second statement describes the different lifetimes of the two areas, which is why objects can outlive the frame that created them.
whys.b: R is relevant: it explains the lifecycle difference.
whys.d: A is true (escape analysis can sometimes avoid heap allocation, but the language model is as stated).

questions.explanation: Each thread has its own stack (StackOverflowError when too deep); the heap is shared (OutOfMemoryError when full).

options.text: 3x12, because 1 + 2 is added before any String appears
options.why: Correct: + is evaluated left to right, so 1 + 2 is integer addition (3) before the first String appears; after that every + is concatenation.

options.text: 12x12, because every + here is string concatenation
options.why: Wrong: this treats every + as concatenation, but the first operands are both ints and are added numerically.

options.text: 3x3, because the trailing 1 + 2 is added numerically
options.why: Wrong: once the left operand is a String, the trailing 1 + 2 is not added; each digit is appended as text.

options.text: Compile error, because int and String cannot be added
options.why: Wrong: the + operator converts non-String operands to text when the other operand is a String.

questions.explanation: Precedence and associativity decide where numeric addition stops and concatenation starts. Also "" + 'a' + 1 gives "a1" but 'a' + 1 + "" gives "98". Verified by running it.

questions.prompt: Match each Java reference type with its behaviour.

right.text: Never cleared while the object is reachable through it; the normal kind
Cleared only when the JVM needs memory, so it suits memory-sensitive caches
Cleared at the next GC once the object has no strong or soft references, as WeakHashMap keys use
get() always returns null; it is enqueued after the object is finalised, for cleanup actions
Cleared the moment the variable holding it goes out of scope

questions.explanation: Soft for caches, weak for canonicalising maps and listener registries, phantom (or java.lang.ref.Cleaner) for post-mortem cleanup. The fifth right item is invented.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: Calling System.gc() guarantees that all unreachable objects are collected immediately.
questions.reason: System.gc() is only a hint, and the JVM is free to ignore it.

whys.a: This option says both statements are true and R explains A, which does not match: A is false because the call is merely a request; R is true.
whys.b: This option says both statements are true but R does not explain A, which does not match: A is false because the call is merely a request; R is true.
whys.c: This option says A is true and R is false, which does not match: A is false because the call is merely a request; R is true.
whys.d: Correct: A is false because the call is merely a request; R is true.

questions.explanation: Never rely on System.gc() for correctness or tune around it; use the right collector and heap settings instead.
